class.name: PXTGI3D
class.experimental: Its look, settings and cost may still change.
class.brief_description: Real-time global illumination traced against the physics shapes (PXTGI), provided by the PhysX module.
class.description: Adds bounce light to the whole scene, every frame, with nothing to bake: light from the sun, [OmniLight3D]s, [SpotLight3D]s and emissive surfaces bounces off what it reaches and colours what is around it, and moving objects take part as they move. Add one node to a scene; where it sits does not matter. Each visible surface sends rays out. A ray first follows what is on screen; where it leaves the screen or passes behind what the screen shows, it continues against the scene's collision shapes ([CollisionShape3D]s of every physics body, static ones included), which stand in for the geometry. So walls, floors and objects only bounce light off-screen if they have collision shapes; a body's colour is taken from its [MeshInstance3D]'s material. Emissive meshes without a body still give off light, as their bounding box. The result is also used for reflections on smooth surfaces (see [member reflection_mode]). Works with the Forward+ renderer only. It uses SDFGI as its switch: while the node is visible it turns on SDFGI in the scene's [Environment] at its cheapest settings (one cascade) and replaces SDFGI's light with its own; hidden or removed, the environment's own SDFGI settings are back. The scene needs an [Environment] (a [WorldEnvironment] or the camera's). Hiding the node turns it off, as with a light: Godot's own lighting is back until it is shown again.

members.member: Shows one stage of the work instead of the lit scene, to see what each adds. [code]0[/code] is off (the normal result).
How strong the bounce light is: [code]1.0[/code] is physically based; higher brightens it artistically.
How far, in metres, rays follow what is on screen before continuing against the collision shapes.

If [code]true[/code], light bounces more than once: surfaces lit by bounce light pass some of it on, filling dark corners and enclosed spaces. If [code]false[/code], one bounce only, which is darker but a little cheaper.

Rays each traced point sends per frame, from [code]1[/code] to [code]4[/code]. More rays settle faster and flicker less when the camera or the lights move, at about proportional cost. [code]2[/code] suits most daylight scenes; scenes lit mostly by emissives or small lights (night) look steadier with [code]4[/code].

Reflections on surfaces smoother than [member reflection_roughness_cutoff]: [code]0[/code] leaves them to Godot (reflection probes, sky, screen-space reflection); [code]1[/code] traces them on screen; [code]2[/code] traces them on screen, then against the collision shapes, so what is behind the camera or off screen is reflected too.

Surfaces at or below this roughness get traced reflections ([member reflection_mode]); rougher ones keep Godot's own reflection (reflection probes, sky). Traced reflections cost per pixel, so a cutoff that includes many common materials costs a lot: at [code]0.5[/code], glossy and mirror-like surfaces are traced, while the broad, blurry reflections of rougher surfaces look the same from a probe.

How far, in metres, rays go against the collision shapes. Shorter is cheaper in large, cluttered scenes, but light from surfaces further than this is not bounced (it falls back to the environment's ambient light). Indoor scenes may look darker if this is shorter than the room.
